props.title: Wise Guys
props.initialSlug: Two mobsters bungle a hit & become targets themselves

sections.content: Wise Guys (1986) represents an often-overlooked entry in the gangster-comedy subgenre, starring Danny DeVito and Joe Piscopo as low-level mobsters who get in over their heads. Director Brian De Palma took a rare comedic turn here, stepping away from his signature psychological thrillers like Dressed to Kill (1980) and Scarface (1983). The film follows a similar path to other mob comedies of the era like Johnny Dangerously (1984) and Oscar (1991), but with De Palma's distinct visual flair occasionally breaking through the broad humor.

sections.content: The 1980s saw a fascinating trend of mob movies playing their subject matter for laughs rather than drama. While The Godfather (1972) and Goodfellas (1990) took serious approaches, films like Wise Guys deliberately subverted gangster movie tropes for comic effect. This era gave us Cookie (1989) with Peter Falk and Oscar (1991) with Sylvester Stallone, both mining humor from mobsters trying to go legitimate.

De Palma's approach in Wise Guys feels like a precursor to later crime comedies like Get Shorty (1995) and The Whole Nine Yards (2000). The film's strength lies in the chemistry between DeVito and Piscopo, even if the material doesn't always serve them well. The movie exists in an interesting space between De Palma's more serious works like Body Double (1984) and pure comedies of the era. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Mob Comedy

sections.content: Wise Guys helped pave the way for more sophisticated crime comedies of the 1990s and beyond. While it may not reach the heights of later entries like Analyze This (1999) or The Family (2013), it demonstrated how gangster film conventions could be successfully played for laughs. The film's influence can be seen in everything from Jane Austen's Mafia! (1998) to The Other Guys (2010).
